title: Taming Steam
summary: Long before trains, people learned that boiling water makes steam strong enough to push heavy things. The first steam engines were giant, slow pumps that stood still and sucked water out of mines. Then clever inventors made them better and smaller, until one day an engine might be able to move itself.

sections.heading: A Problem Full of Water
paragraphs: To understand why anyone bothered to invent a steam engine, you have to climb down a mine. Imagine standing at the bottom of a coal pit in the English Midlands around the year 1700. It is dark, cold and dripping. Every few minutes you hear water trickling out of the rock walls, collecting in puddles, then pools, then something closer to an underground pond. The deeper the miners dig, the more water seeps in. If nobody gets it out, the mine floods and all the coal at the bottom is lost.

By the late 1600s this was one of the biggest headaches in British industry. Coal was replacing wood as the main fuel for homes, forges and breweries, because many forests had already been cut down. Tin and copper mines in Cornwall faced the same trouble. The easy, shallow seams near the surface had been dug out long ago, so miners had to go deeper, and deeper meant wetter.

The old ways of draining a mine were slow and expensive. Teams of men turned handles. Horses walked round and round in circles, turning a big wheel called a horse gin that pulled up buckets on chains. Some mines dug long drainage tunnels, called adits or soughs, sloping gently downhill to let water run out into a valley. Where there was a fast stream, a waterwheel could drive pumps. But a big mine might need dozens of horses working in shifts, and every horse had to be fed, stabled and replaced. Some mines simply gave up.

So the question that haunted mine owners was simple: was there a tireless machine that could lift water, day and night, without eating hay? The answer would come from a pot of boiling water. And although nobody knew it yet, the machine invented to solve this underground problem would one day, about a hundred years later, start rolling along rails.

People had played with the power of steam for a very long time. Hero of Alexandria, a Greek engineer living in Roman Egypt in the first century CE, described a spinning ball pushed round by jets of steam, but it was a curiosity, not a working machine. In the 1600s scientists in Italy, Germany, France and England began experimenting seriously with air pressure and vacuums. They discovered that the air around us presses on everything with surprising force, and that if you could make an empty space, a vacuum, the outside air would push hard to fill it. That discovery was the key that unlocked the first steam engines.

One early attempt came from Thomas Savery, an English military engineer, who patented a steam pump in 1698 and nicknamed it the 'Miner's Friend'. It had no piston. Instead, steam filled a metal vessel, was cooled to make a partial vacuum, and the vacuum sucked water up a pipe. Then fresh steam pushed the water further up. It was a clever idea, but in practice it could only suck water up about 30 feet (around 9 metres), it used lots of fuel, and its joints were dangerous under pressure. A French scientist, Denis Papin, had meanwhile shown that steam condensing under a piston could make that piston move, but he never built a full-size working engine. Someone needed to combine these ideas into a machine that really worked.

sections.heading: Newcomen's Giant Nodding Beam
paragraphs: That someone was Thomas Newcomen, an ironmonger from Dartmouth, a small port in Devon in south-west England. We do not even know his exact birthday, only that he was born around 1664. He sold tools and iron goods, and many of his customers were tin mines in Devon and Cornwall, so he heard about their flooding problems all the time. Newcomen was a Baptist, which meant he belonged to a church outside the official Church of England, and in those days that kept people like him out of the universities. He taught himself, and he worked closely with a plumber and glazier named John Calley.

After years of trial and error, Newcomen and Calley built their first known working engine in 1712, near Dudley Castle in the English Midlands, to pump water from a coal mine. It is often called the first practical steam engine in the world. A picture of it survives: an engraving made in 1719 by Thomas Barney, showing a tall engine house with a huge wooden beam sticking out of the top like a giant seesaw.

Here is how it worked, and it is cleverer than it first looks. At the bottom of the engine house sat a boiler, a big copper or iron pot over a coal fire, making steam at hardly more than the normal pressure of the air. Above the boiler stood an upright cylinder, open at the top, with a piston inside that could slide up and down. The piston was connected by a chain to one end of the great wooden beam. The other end of the beam was connected to long, heavy pump rods hanging down the mine shaft.

Because the pump rods were heavy, their weight pulled their end of the beam down, which lifted the piston to the top of the cylinder. As the piston rose, steam from the boiler flowed in underneath it. Then came the magic moment: a jet of cold water was sprayed into the cylinder. The steam instantly turned back into a few drops of water, leaving almost empty space, a partial vacuum. Now the air outside, pressing down on the open top of the piston, shoved the piston down into the cylinder with enormous force. The beam rocked, the other end swung up, and the pump rods rose, lifting water out of the mine. Then steam was let in again, and the whole cycle repeated.

This is why Newcomen's machine is called an atmospheric engine. The steam did not really push anything. It was just a way of making a vacuum. The real muscle was the weight of the atmosphere itself, pressing down at about 1 kilogram on every square centimetre, which adds up to roughly 10 tonnes on every square metre. A big piston could feel tonnes of force.

The Dudley Castle engine nodded about 12 times a minute and is reported to have pumped around 120 gallons (about 550 litres) of water every minute. That may sound slow, but it kept going hour after hour, and it could lift water from far deeper than Savery's pump. Mine owners were thrilled. Within about 20 years, more than 120 Newcomen engines had been built in Britain and Europe, and by 1800 there were over 1,400 of them.

sections.heading: Big, Hungry and Rooted to the Spot
paragraphs: Newcomen's engine changed mining, but it was nothing like a train engine. For a start, it was enormous. The engine was built into its own stone engine house, several storeys tall, and the building itself was part of the machine, holding up the beam. Engines were built more like houses than like gadgets. Cylinders were cast by the same foundries that made cannons, and the rest was put together by carpenters, stonemasons and blacksmiths using traditional skills.

You can see just how big these machines were at the Science Museum in London, which displays a Newcomen-type engine built in 1791 by Francis Thompson and last used at Pentrich in Derbyshire. Together with parts of its engine house it weighs about 105 tonnes. It is a late example, with a cast-iron beam, because earlier engines used massive wooden beams. In Newcomen's home town of Dartmouth you can see a real engine dating from 1725, and the Black Country Living Museum near Dudley has built a working full-size replica of the 1712 engine, based on old engravings and records. It was completed in 1986.

The second problem was fuel. Every time cold water was sprayed into the cylinder, it cooled the cylinder walls down. Then the next puff of steam had to heat the cold metal up again before it could fill the cylinder, and much of the steam was wasted just doing that. A Newcomen engine gobbled coal. At a coal mine this did not matter much, because the engine could burn cheap, low-quality coal that nobody wanted to buy anyway. At a Cornish tin mine, where coal had to be shipped in from Wales, the fuel bill was painful.

The third problem was the most important for our story: the engine could not move. It was fixed to the ground, fixed to its building and fixed to its mine shaft. It made a slow up-and-down motion, perfect for working a pump but not for turning wheels. Nobody in 1712 imagined that such a machine might ever roll along a road. Still, Newcomen engines kept working for an astonishingly long time. Some were still pumping mines well into the 1800s, a century after the first one was built.

sections.heading: James Watt's Walk on Glasgow Green
paragraphs: Fifty years after Dudley Castle, the next big leap happened in Scotland. James Watt, born in 1736 in Greenock on the River Clyde, was a skilled maker of scientific instruments working at the University of Glasgow. Around 1763 to 1764, the university asked him to repair a small model of a Newcomen engine used for teaching. The model worked badly. It would run for a few strokes and then run out of steam, even though its boiler seemed big enough.

Watt did what good scientists do: he measured things. He found that the problem was the one we have just met. Most of the steam was being wasted heating up the cylinder again after each cold spray. The cylinder was being heated and cooled, heated and cooled, dozens of times a minute. Watt realised that to save fuel, the cylinder needed to stay hot all the time, while the steam still needed to be cooled to make a vacuum. Those two wishes seemed to contradict each other.

The answer came to him, according to his own later account, on a Sunday afternoon walk across Glasgow Green in May 1765. Why not cool the steam somewhere else? He imagined a separate chamber, a condenser, connected to the cylinder by a pipe and kept cold all the time. When a valve opened, the steam would rush out of the hot cylinder into the cold condenser and turn to water there, leaving a vacuum behind it in the cylinder, while the cylinder itself stayed hot. It was a simple idea, but it took years of hard work to turn it into a reliable machine.

Watt's patent for the separate condenser was granted in 1769. At first his business partner, John Roebuck, ran into money trouble and went bankrupt. Then the Birmingham manufacturer Matthew Boulton took over Roebuck's share, and in 1775 the famous partnership of Boulton and Watt was formed at Boulton's Soho works near Birmingham. That same year Parliament extended Watt's patent so that it would last until 1800. The first Boulton and Watt engines went to work in 1776, mostly pumping mines.

The results were dramatic. A Watt engine could do the same work as a Newcomen engine while burning far less coal, and some estimates say Watt's design was up to about five times as fuel-efficient. Boulton and Watt often charged mine owners a share of the money they saved on coal, which shows just how big the savings were. Cornish mines, with their expensive imported coal, quickly became some of their best customers.

Watt kept improving his engines. He added ways to make the piston push in both directions, and with his team he developed gears that turned the up-and-down motion of the beam into turning motion, so engines could drive machines in factories, mills and breweries, not just pumps. He even made popular the idea of measuring an engine's power in 'horsepower', comparing it to the number of horses it could replace. Today the scientific unit of power, the watt, is named after him. Every light bulb label that says '10 W' is a tiny tribute to James Watt.

But Watt had one firm rule. His engines worked with steam at only a little above the pressure of the air. Boilers in the 1700s were made of riveted plates of iron or copper, and they could burst. A bursting boiler sprays scalding steam and flying metal, and it can kill. Watt considered higher-pressure steam too dangerous, and he and Boulton argued against it. With his patent in force until 1800, the firm also had legal power to stop rival engineers from building engines with separate condensers. This caution made sense for a factory engine bolted to a floor. As we will see, it also helped hold back the idea of an engine that could move.

sections.heading: Cugnot's Steam Cart
paragraphs: While British engineers were busy pumping mines, a French army engineer was thinking about something much bolder. Nicolas-Joseph Cugnot was born in 1725 in Void, a village in Lorraine in eastern France. He served as a military engineer and wrote books about fortifications and war machines. The French army had a very practical problem: its cannons were extremely heavy, and dragging them around with teams of horses was slow and difficult. Could steam do the job instead?

Cugnot tested a small model in 1769, and in 1770 a full-size machine was built. It was called a fardier à vapeur, which means 'steam dray'. A fardier was a big, sturdy cart used for hauling heavy loads such as cannon barrels. Cugnot's version had three wheels: two at the back and one at the front. Hanging out in front of the front wheel was a large round copper boiler with a firebox under it, and two cylinders whose pistons were pushed directly by the steam. Through a ratchet mechanism, the pistons turned the single front wheel.

It was a strange-looking beast. Empty, it weighed about 2.5 tonnes. All the weight of the boiler hung over the front wheel, so steering it was very hard work, a bit like trying to push a wheelbarrow loaded with bricks round a corner. It was slow, too. It was meant to cover several kilometres in an hour, but in practice it crawled along at little more than walking pace. Worst of all, its boiler could not make steam fast enough, so every quarter of an hour or so it had to stop and wait for the pressure to build up again.

There is a famous story that in 1771 Cugnot's machine crashed into a wall in Paris, making it 'the first car accident in history'. It is a good story, but it is only a legend. Historians have found no record of it written at the time; it first appears in print decades later. What is true is that the army lost interest. Cugnot was given a pension of 600 livres a year by King Louis XV in 1772. He lost it during the French Revolution, and Napoleon restored it shortly before Cugnot died in Paris in 1804.

Cugnot's fardier still exists. Since 1800 it has been kept at the Conservatoire national des arts et métiers in Paris, and it is now displayed in the Musée des Arts et Métiers there. It is often described as the oldest surviving self-propelled land vehicle in the world. In 2010, engineering students in France built a working replica to test how it really behaved. Cugnot's steam cart never ran on rails and never carried passengers on a regular route, but it showed something important: a steam engine could be made small enough to travel along with the load it was moving.

sections.heading: Murdoch's Little Runaway Carriage
paragraphs: Back in Britain, one of the most talented engineers of the age was working inside the very company that disliked high-pressure steam. William Murdoch was born in 1754 in Ayrshire, Scotland, the son of a millwright. In 1777 he travelled south to Birmingham to ask for a job at Boulton and Watt. There is a popular story that he impressed Matthew Boulton by wearing a hat he had turned himself out of wood on a lathe. Nobody can prove it, but it fits his inventive character.

Boulton and Watt soon sent Murdoch to Cornwall to put up and look after their engines in the mining district around Redruth. He lived there for many years from 1779, working long hours climbing around engine houses and fixing problems. In his spare time, he built something remarkable: a small model steam carriage. In 1784 it was seen running around his living room in Redruth. It was only a model, small enough to pick up, but it moved under its own steam, using steam at higher pressure than Boulton and Watt's big engines.

A much-told tale says that one night Murdoch tested the little carriage on a dark lane near the church. It hissed off on its own, glowing and puffing, and frightened the local vicar, who thought he had met the Devil himself. Like Cugnot's crash, this is a story rather than a proven fact, and if it happened at all, it probably involved the model rather than a full-size carriage. But it shows how strange a self-moving, fire-breathing machine must have seemed to people at the time.

James Watt was not impressed. He thought steam carriages had no future, and he also worried about losing his best engineer in Cornwall. When Murdoch set off for London in 1785, intending to patent his carriage, Matthew Boulton met him on the way and persuaded him to go back to Cornwall and forget about it. Murdoch stayed loyal to the firm for the rest of his career and later became a partner. He went on to other great achievements: in the 1790s he pioneered lighting with coal gas, and he is credited with the 'sun and planet' gear that helped Watt's engines turn wheels. His model steam carriage survives today at Thinktank, Birmingham's science museum.

Redruth is only a few kilometres from Camborne, and in the 1780s a tall Cornish boy was growing up nearby among the engine houses. Some historians have wondered whether he ever saw or heard about Murdoch's little carriage. We do not know. But that boy would soon take up the idea that Watt had turned down.

sections.heading: The Science of Steam: Why Pressure Was the Key
paragraphs: Let us stop and look closely at the science, because it explains why the next part of our story happened. When you heat water in a kettle, the water molecules move faster and faster. At 100 degrees Celsius, at normal air pressure, they move fast enough to break away and fly off as a gas: steam. Here is the astonishing part. When water turns into steam at normal air pressure, it takes up about 1,600 times as much space. One cupful of water becomes enough steam to fill a large bucket hundreds of times over.

Now imagine trapping that steam in a closed box. The steam wants to spread out, so it presses hard on every wall of the box. If one wall of the box can move, like a piston sliding in a cylinder, the steam will push it. That is the basic idea behind every steam engine that pushes with steam: heat makes water into steam, steam presses, and the press moves a piston. You can see a tiny version of this when the lid of a saucepan rattles and jumps as the water boils underneath.

If you keep heating the water inside a strong, closed boiler, the pressure keeps rising. Higher pressure steam pushes harder on every square centimetre. And the force on a piston equals the pressure multiplied by the area of the piston. That simple rule is the whole secret. If you double the pressure, you can get the same push from a piston with half the area. If you make the pressure several times higher, you can make the whole engine much smaller and lighter while getting just as much power.

Compare two ways of making an engine. A Newcomen engine, or a low-pressure Watt engine, relied heavily on the vacuum made by condensing steam. The most force it could ever get from the air pressing on the piston was limited to about 1 kilogram per square centimetre. To get a big force, it needed a huge piston, a huge cylinder, a huge beam and a condenser fed with lots of cold water. Imagine trying to fit all that, plus a water tank and a cooling system, onto a cart. It was hopeless.

A high-pressure engine does things differently. Its boiler makes 'strong steam', at pressures several times higher than the air around it, and lets that steam push the piston directly. After the steam has done its work, it is simply let out into the open air. There is no condenser, no cooling water, no giant beam. The used steam escapes in short, sharp bursts, which is why such engines were nicknamed 'puffers'. A high-pressure engine could be small enough to sit on a cart, and powerful enough to move the cart, and its load, and itself.

There was a catch, of course: danger. A boiler full of high-pressure steam stores a great deal of energy, like a balloon blown up much too tight. If it bursts, all that energy escapes at once. So high-pressure engines needed strong boilers, carefully made, and safety devices such as safety valves, which open and let steam out if the pressure climbs too high. James Watt's fear was not silly; boilers did explode, and people were killed. But the reward for taming high-pressure steam safely was enormous: an engine light enough to move. The world needed someone brave, skilled and stubborn enough to try.

sections.heading: Waiting for a Daring Engineer
paragraphs: By the end of the 1700s, all the pieces were lying on the table. Newcomen had shown that steam could do heavy work, every day, for years. Watt had shown how to make engines far more efficient and how to turn their motion into turning wheels. Cugnot had shown that a steam engine could travel with its load, even if clumsily. Murdoch had shown, in a living room in Redruth, that a small high-pressure engine could drive a carriage. And the wagonways of Part 2 had shown that heavy loads glide easily along smooth rails.

Two things still stood in the way. One was a legal fence: Watt's patent on the separate condenser lasted until 1800, and Boulton and Watt defended it fiercely against anyone they thought was copying it. The other was a fence in people's minds: the belief that high-pressure steam was simply too dangerous to use. In 1800 the patent finally ran out. The legal fence was gone. Now someone had to jump the second fence.

That someone was living in Cornwall, in the mining country between Camborne and Redruth. He was very tall, famously strong, impatient with schoolwork but brilliant with machines, the son of a mine captain who had grown up surrounded by the thump and hiss of pumping engines. He had already argued with Boulton and Watt about his own engine designs. And unlike the great James Watt, he was not afraid of high-pressure steam at all. His name was Richard Trevithick.

deepDive: Historians of technology often say the steam engine was not one invention but a long chain of improvements, and Part 3 shows why. The Newcomen engine of 1712 relied on atmospheric pressure, about 101 kilopascals at sea level, acting on one side of a piston while condensing steam created a partial vacuum on the other. Because the same cylinder was alternately heated and cooled, a great deal of heat was thrown away on every stroke. Watt's separate condenser, conceived in 1765 and patented in 1769, attacked exactly this loss, and his engines are often said to have used something like a quarter to a fifth of the fuel of a comparable Newcomen engine. Even so, by modern standards these machines were wildly inefficient: early Newcomen engines turned only around 1 percent of the energy in their coal into useful work, and Watt's best engines reached only a few percent. The deeper science explaining why was not understood until the 1820s and later, when Sadi Carnot and others founded thermodynamics, partly by asking why steam engines worked as they did. Historians also debate the role of patents. Watt's patent, extended by Parliament to 1800, gave Boulton and Watt the security to invest in a risky business, but critics argue that the firm also used it to block rival designs, including high-pressure engines, for decades. Some economic historians suggest that steam engineering advanced faster after 1800, once the patent expired and engineers such as Richard Trevithick and Arthur Woolf were free to experiment. Another debate concerns 'firsts'. Cugnot's 1770 vehicle is often called the first automobile, and it is certainly the oldest surviving self-propelled land vehicle, yet it had little direct influence on later steam transport in Britain. Murdoch's 1784 model may or may not have inspired Trevithick; the two lived near each other, but there is no firm evidence of a connection. Finally, the figure of about 1,600 for the expansion of water into steam applies at normal atmospheric pressure; at higher pressures steam is denser, which is precisely why a strong boiler can store so much energy, and so much danger.
funFact: James Watt made 'horsepower' the standard way of rating engines, so that customers could compare his machines with the horses they were replacing, and the unit of power called the watt was later named in his honour.

check.q: What was James Watt's big improvement to the Newcomen steam engine?
check.a: A separate condenser, so the cylinder could stay hot and much less fuel was wasted

Replacing the wooden beam with a rope pulled by horses
